An app protection policy protects data inside managed apps (blocking copy-paste to personal apps, requiring a PIN) and works whether or not the device is enrolled, whereas a device compliance policy evaluates the device and that verdict can gate access through Conditional Access. Use app protection for BYOD where you cannot manage the hardware.

A compliance policy lives in Intune and decides whether a device meets your standards. A Conditional Access policy lives in Entra and decides whether an access attempt is allowed, and it can use signals such as user, location, risk and device state to make that decision. One evaluates the device, the other protects access to it, and most tenants use both working together.

A compliance policy judges a device: it defines rules such as minimum OS version, encryption or password strength, then marks each device compliant or noncompliant, and that verdict can gate access through Conditional Access. A configuration profile changes a device: it pushes settings like Wi-Fi, VPN, certificates or restrictions. One evaluates, the other configures, and most tenants use both together.

A device group targets the machine regardless of who signs in, which suits kiosk, shared or unattended devices, and a user group targets the person across every device they use, which suits app and data policies. Assigning the wrong one is a common cause of policies appearing not to apply, so it is important to get the assignment correct before you proceed.

A security baseline is a Microsoft-published bundle of recommended security settings you can assign as a starting point; a configuration profile is one you build yourself. Baselines save you deciding hundreds of settings; profiles let you express a requirement a vendor or partner hands you, or a one the app asks for, as a managed device feature rather than a bundle someone else has already decided.
